name: Sara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do Spanish–English subtitles for a tiny documentary studio, three people in a converted garage, and I localise small indie video games, which means translating menus, dialogue and jokes so they still work. I run every script through an AI tool first, then spend the day fixing timing, tone and the jokes it ruins. I love the games work, because a good pun in a menu feels like a small win. What tires me out is chasing invoices; one studio paid me ninety days late last year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things set up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house with two nurses who work nights, so the kitchen is mine during the day. I've got about two weeks of money saved, because a laptop repair ate the rest. My rates are on the low side, since I'm still building a portfolio and there are no studios in my town, so it's all online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the AI tools are useful but overhyped, which is what I already say. Online I'd post side-by-side clips of a joke the machine translated straight and the one I rewrote. People love those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in this picture I'm okay. My two regular clients like that I'm fast because of the tools, and the games keep coming. My worry is the late invoices and having only two weeks of money, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to take on more games, maybe one extra project a month. I'd start charging a late fee in my contracts and ask for half up front, which I've been too shy to do. And I'd open a separate account and move ten percent of each invoice into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small itch at the back of my head about money. It's the itch every freelancer has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're too shy to ask for half up front. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm scared they'll just go to someone cheaper. The games world is full of students who'll do it for exposure, and I was one of them two years ago. But the studio that paid me ninety days late is the reason I'm now sharing a kitchen at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in this picture make you leave translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If AI is just a fancy helper, I'm the person who's best at using the helper. I'd stay and try to get my rates up.

say: AI tools are **useful but overhyped**, which is what I already say.
I'd post **side-by-side clips** of machine jokes and my rewrites.
think: My two **regular clients** like that the tools make me fast.
My real worry is **late invoices** and only two weeks of savings.
do: Take on **one extra game** a month using the tools.
Add a **late fee** and ask for half up front in contracts.
Move **ten percent** of each invoice into a separate account.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a freelancer's itch about money.
S0.quote: If AI is just a fancy helper, I'm the person who's best at using the helper.
fieldNote: She sees AI tools as **her edge**, not a threat, in this picture.
Her stress comes from **late payment**, not from technology.
She knows she **undercharges** out of fear of cheaper students.

steps.text: Take on one extra indie game project each month
Use AI drafts to speed up subtitle timing and dialogue
Move ten percent of every invoice into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to become the people who check, shape and sign off the AI's work, and that we should be paid for it properly. I'd push for the subtitlers' group I'm in to publish fair rates for that. I'd also say loudly that studios should credit the human, not just the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the documentary subtitles go first, because the studio can run them through software for nothing. The games work holds longer, because jokes and character voices are hard. I'd lose maybe a third of my income in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn a bit of scripting so I can build checking tools for game text, and pitch myself as a localisation lead, the person who runs the AI and a couple of freelancers. I'd also start a small online course teaching other translators how I use the tools, as a side income. If that doesn't work, I'd ask the studio about project coordinator work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit excited, which is a strange mix. I'd lose something, but there's a door I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach other translators to use the tools that are shrinking their work. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortably. I'd tell them straight that it won't save everyone, and I'd keep the course cheap. But pretending the AI tools aren't there helps nobody, least of all translators with no savings, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost a third of your income, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gym, my streaming, and the trip home for my cousin's wedding, which would really hurt. My room rent is fixed, so the cuts come from everything that's actually fun. I'd eat a lot of rice.

Studios must **credit the human**, not only the software.
think: **Documentary subtitles** go first because software does them for nothing.
I'd lose about **a third** of my income in the first year.

Pitch herself as a **localisation lead** running AI and freelancers.
Sell a cheap **online course** on using the tools.
feel: **Nervous and excited**, seeing a door through the loss.
S1.quote: Pretending the AI tools aren't there helps nobody, least of all translators with no savings, like me.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose a third** of income but sees a route to lead roles.
She is **uneasy** about teaching others the tools that shrink their work.
Her cuts fall on **fun and family trips**, since rent is fixed.

steps.text: Learn basic scripting to build checking tools for game text

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income right now, not in a report next year. I'd be online every day pushing for it, and I'd join the protests. I'd also say plainly that anyone telling young translators to just upskill is lying to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, all my skills become worthless in two years, including the AI ones. Running the AI is a thinking job too, and the AI runs itself. The robots coming later in 2031 doesn't help, because I've never done a hands-on job in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sell my second monitor and the good headphones and go back to living with my mum to stop paying rent. I'd take any in-person work I could find, a café or a warehouse, for the three years before the robots. And I'd volunteer for the basic income campaign, because that's where my hope would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is going. I'm usually the one who's ahead, and in a two-year world being ahead means nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being ahead means nothing. Is there anything your AI skills would still buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few months. I could probably get a short contract helping a studio switch fully over to AI, which is a horrible thought. I'd take it, because rent is rent, and then I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum it's temporary and that I'm part of a movement, which sounds braver than it is. She'd ask if I've eaten, and I'd cry. Then I'd set up a desk in my old bedroom and start writing to my local representative.

Telling young translators to **just upskill** is a lie.
think: All my skills, even the **AI ones**, become worthless in two years.

feel: Like the **floor is going**, when she's used to being ahead.
S2.quote: I'm usually the one who's ahead, and in a two-year world being ahead means nothing.
fieldNote: Her adaptability gives **no shelter** when AI runs itself.
She would still take a **switch-over contract**, then leave, out of need.

steps.text: Sell her second monitor and studio headphones
Move back into her mum's home to stop paying rent
Take café or warehouse shifts until robots arrive
Volunteer for the basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a clear warning, and young freelancers need a plan from the government now. I'd keep sharing how to use the tools, but I'd add that this is about whole careers ending. I'd be one of the louder voices in the subtitling group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd ride the AI wave for two or three years and earn better than I ever have, as a localisation lead. Then it ends for me too, around 2031. The trick is saving during the good years, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every AI-heavy project I can for two years and save half of the extra money, aiming for six months of savings by 2029. At the same time I'd start a part-time course in something people-facing, maybe speech therapy, which mixes languages and being in the room. I'd also join a union, since freelancers will need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but focused. With five years I'd feel like I'm running a race against my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Speech therapy. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It uses everything I love about language, but you're sitting with a child or a stroke patient, watching their mouth. That's hands-on in a way, and the robots for that would come later. My aunt had a stroke, and the therapist was the only person who made her laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is saving half of the extra money realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, not without a trick. I'd set it to move automatically on the day an invoice lands, before I see it. If I see it, I spend it on the trip home.

fieldNote: She sees a **short boom** for herself before the work ends.
**Speech therapy** links her love of language to hands-on care.
She knows she needs **automatic saving** to stop herself spending.

steps.text: Take every AI-heavy localisation project for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. I'd campaign for free retraining for anyone whose job AI takes. I'd sound more hopeful than in the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's almost a good picture for me. I get several years as a localisation lead, then time to qualify as a speech therapist by my mid-thirties. The risk is getting comfortable and forgetting the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on AI localisation for the next four years and save properly. Around 2030 I'd start speech therapy training full-time, using the savings to cover the gap. I'd also start mentoring younger translators, because someone needs to tell them the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a quiet worry underneath. Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast the last three went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said almost a good picture. What's the 'almost'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 'almost' is my savings. I've never had more than a month, and a full-time course needs a year of rent. If I mess up the saving, the plan falls apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do games localisation in 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably as a hobby, for fun. By then the studios won't need me, but I'd still translate jokes for friends' games, because I love it. That's the bit nobody can automate: wanting to.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind.
Anyone whose job AI takes should get **free retraining**.
think: It's **almost a good picture**, with lead work and then speech therapy.
The risk is getting **comfortable** and forgetting the date.
do: Work hard on **AI localisation** for four years and save properly.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a quiet worry about how fast time goes.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast the last three went.
fieldNote: Her plan hinges on **saving a year's rent**, which she has never done.
She keeps **anxious** mood because her income still ends and savings are thin.

steps.text: Lead AI localisation projects for indie games until 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because nothing I've learned would matter and I'd be back in my old bedroom. What would help is a basic income that starts before people lose everything, not after. And honest advice for young people, not upskilling slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the jokes. The machine can translate a joke now, but it can't tell when a joke has stopped being funny in another country. The day it can, I'll believe the rest.

headlineQuote: The machine can translate a joke now, but it can't tell when a joke has stopped being funny in another country.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** Spanish–English subtitler and indie games localiser who uses AI every day.
She rents a room in a shared house and has about **two weeks** of savings after late invoices.
She sees the tools as **her edge** and plans to lead AI localisation, then train in speech therapy.
Her progressive views push her towards **basic income** campaigning when the fast pictures leave no personal plan.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and stays anxious even with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, where all her skills stop mattering and she moves back home.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** that starts before people lose everything.
**Honest advice** for young people instead of upskilling slogans.
